Leading with  
Excellence
Innovating for  
the Future
For over five decades, Cochin Shipyard Limited 
(CSL) has stood at the helm of India’s maritime 
journey, anchored in engineering excellence, 
propelled by innovation and guided by an 
unswerving commitment to nation-building. 
From building the country’s first 
Indigenous Aircraft Carrier to delivering 
world-class hybrid and electric-powered 
vessels, CSL has consistently pushed 
the boundaries in shipbuilding, repair 
and marine engineering.
As we navigate a dynamic global 
maritime landscape, our focus remains 
on crafting future-ready solutions that 
are smart, sustainable and strategic. 
Whether it is investing in cutting-edge 
infrastructure, delivering complex 
defence projects or adopting green 
technologies, we are reimagining 
shipbuilding to meet future needs.Driven by a skilled workforce 
and empowered by a culture 
of continuous learning and 
collaboration, CSL continues to 
chart bold new courses at home and 
across international waters. We are 
building capabilities, partnerships 
and a resilient maritime future for 
India and the world.Forward-looking statements

Terramaris: The Eternal Symbol 
of CSL’s Legacy
Conceived as an energy point within CSL, 
the sculpture represents the progressive 
evolution of the Shipyard, embracing 
change, harnessing the power of its 
people, and embodying the essence 
of the sea and shipbuilding. Designed 
to endure for the next 1000 years, this 
monumental structure is more than 
an artistic marvel—it is a beacon of 
inspiration, igniting internal energy and 
fueling CSL’s ambitions for the future.
A Vision Cast in Metal and 
Stone
Crafted under the artistic genius of 
Shri P V Ramachandran, also known A Legacy Set in Stone  
and Copper
The realization of this historic 
project was marked by three 
key milestones: 
 April 30, 2022 – Hon’ble Union 
Minister for Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways, Shri Sarbananda 
Sonowal, inaugurated CSL’s 
Golden Jubilee celebrations 
by digitally unveiling the 
sculpture’s design.
 November 30, 2024 – The 
sculpture was successfully 
completed, earning prestigious 
recognition in the Asia Book 
of Records and India Book of 
Records for its grandeur and 
unique craftsmanship
 April 07, 2025 – Hon’ble Union 
Minister for Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways, Shri Sarbananda 
Sonowal, dedicated the 
sculpture, commemorating the 
50th anniversary of CSL.As Cochin Shipyard Limited celebrated its Golden Jubilee, a grand 
vision was set in motion—one that would transcend time, inspire 
generations, and stand as a testament to the indomitable spirit of 
the Shipyard. This vision materialized in the form of a magnificent 
sculpture named Terramaris, an awe-inspiring tribute to the 
workforce that has propelled CSL ’s journey of excellence.
as Maraprabhu Ramachandran, the 
sculpture captures the convergence 
of kinetic and potential energies, 
symbolizing the creative and 
constructive spirit of CSL’s workforce. It 
also serves as a solemn homage to the 
maritime pioneers, whose innovations 
have shaped the modern shipping 
industry. This sculpture has been 
designed in accordance with the Golden 
Ratio and has been vetted by Professor 
Sunny Kuriakose. Standing 28.5 feet 
tall, the sculpture features a stainless 
steel (SS 316) framework, covered with 
exquisite copper sheeting, meticulously 
handcrafted by the master artisans of Venkala Paithruka Gramam, Ezhimala, 
Kannur. The granite-clad foundation, 
the intricately designed podium, and 
the ornamental copper embellishments 
elevate its grandeur, making it an 
unparalleled masterpiece in CSL’s history. 
Strategically positioned on the western 
side of CSL’s Main Office building, the 
sculpture commands visibility, ensuring 
that its symbolism remains etched in 
the hearts of every employee, visitor, 
and maritime enthusiast who walks 
through the Shipyard.
A Timeless Symbol  
of Progress
With Terramaris, CSL has not 
only immortalized its past but 
has also laid the foundation 
for the future—a future where 
tradition meets innovation, art 
meets engineering, and history 
meets eternity. This monumental 
sculpture stands as an unwavering 
testament to CSL’s commitment to 
excellence, echoing the Shipyard’s 
motto: Always Moving Forward, 
Always Evolving.

About us
Charting India’s Maritime Future 
with Excellence and Innovation
Over the years, we have built and 
repaired some of the largest and most 
advanced ships in India, including 
the construction of country’s first 
Indigenous Aircraft Carrier, INS Vikrant. 
Our reputation extends globally, having 
exported vessels to some of the most 
demanding clients in countries such 
as Norway, Netherlands, Cyprus, USA, 
Germany, Bahamas, Saudi Arabia, Liberia 
and UAE. We have collaborated with 
global firms including Rolls Royce Marine 
(Norway), GTT (France), Vard Group 
(Norway), IHC Holland BV (Netherlands), 
Robert Allan Limited (Canada), and 
Conoship International BV (Netherlands). 
We have also delivered sustainable 
solutions like hybrid and electric 
vessels to domestic and international 
clients, reinforcing our commitment 
to environmental responsibility. CSL With over five decades of maritime legacy, Cochin Shipyard has 
emerged as a national leader in shipbuilding and ship repair, driven 
by engineering excellence and a strong commitment to innovation. 
Incorporated in 1972, we have consistently responded to the 
evolving needs of the industry, delivering a wide array of vessels 
to both defence and commercial sectors. Our state-of-the-art 
infrastructure, backed by a skilled and dedicated workforce, enables 
us to execute complex projects with precision and reliability.
is also actively engaged in repairs, 
upgrades, and maintenance of various 
vessel types, including ships in the oil 
exploration sector.
As a Schedule A CPSE (Central Public 
Sector Enterprise) under the Ministry 
of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, we 
are proud of our growing international 
presence, collaborations with leading 
global players, and our ability to adapt 
to market shifts. Our unswerving focus 
on R&D, clean energy transition and 
indigenisation positions us to contribute 
meaningfully to the Government’s 
maritime ambitions under the Maritime 
India Vision (MIV) 2030 and the Maritime 
Amrit Kaal Vision (MAKV) 2047.Vision
 Emerge as an internationally 
preferred shipyard to construct 
world class Merchant and 
Naval ships, offshore vessels 
and structures.
 Be the market leader in India for 
ship repairs, including conversions 
and upgradation.
 To be admired for our 
achievements, respected for 
our ethics and trusted for 
our service excellence by our 
valued customers.

Chairman’s message
Dear shareholders, 
It is with immense pleasure that I present to 
you the performance highlights of Cochin 
Shipyard Limited (CSL) for the financial year 
2024–25, a year marked by record turnover, 
Profit Before Tax (PBT) and Profit After Tax 
(PAT), good execution and significant progress 
across strategic priorities. We strengthened 
our presence in defence, commercial and 
green vessel segments, while expanding 
our international footprint through key 
collaborations. The commencement of 
operations at major infrastructure projects 
viz., the New Dry Dock and the International 
Ship Repair Facility has enhanced our 
capacity to execute complex and high-value 
assignments. With a diversified order book 
and a clear focus on operational excellence, 
CSL continues to contribute meaningfully to 
the nation’s maritime growth story.
Financial performance 
I am pleased to share that CSL achieved its 
highest-ever turnover, PBT and PAT both in 
terms of standalone and consolidated basis in 
the financial year 2024–25, marking another 
significant milestone in the Company’s growth 
journey. On a consolidated basis CSL  recorded 
a turnover of ₹4,820 Crores in FY 2024-25 
compared to ₹3,830 Crores in FY 2023–24. 
Shipbuilding income reported was ₹2,955 
Crores, while the ship repair income was 
₹1,865 Crores. Profit Before Tax increased 
to ₹1,125 Crores from ₹1,071 Crores in the 
previous year. Profit After Tax for the year was 
₹827 Crores compared to ₹783 Crores in  
FY 2023–24. The Company’s net worth  
increased to ₹5579 Crores as on March 31, 2025.
The Board has recommended a final dividend 
of ₹2.25 per equity share on the 26,30,80,780 
fully paid equity shares of ₹5 each. Earlier, 
interim dividends of ₹4.00 and ₹3.50 per 
equity share, aggregating to ₹7.50 per equity 
share, had been paid to the shareholders 
during the year. This takes the total dividend 
for FY 2024–25 to ₹9.75 per equity share 
(195%), amounting to ₹256.50 Crores.
Further, the Government of India in October 
2024, divested 4.95% of its stake in CSL 
through Offer for Sale (OFS), increasing the 
public float to 32.09% with Government of 
India retaining the balance 67.91%.
Operational performance 
During FY 2024-25, CSL maintained steady 
operational performance. In shipbuilding, CSL received an order from a European client to 
design and build a Hybrid Service Operation 
Vessel (SOV). This vessel, equipped with 
hybrid battery systems, is aimed at improving 
energy efficiency and reducing emissions, 
and will support the service and maintenance 
needs of offshore wind farms in the European 
market, where sustainable energy solutions 
are gaining momentum. CSL also signed an 
agreement with Kochi Municipal Corporation 
for constructing a Ro-Ro Vessel. While the 
project may not be large in financial terms, it 
has great value for society by helping reduce 
traffic, save travel time, and encourage eco-
friendly transport in Kochi. 
During the year, CSL delivered five Hybrid 
Electric Catamaran Hull Vessels to Kochi water 
metro project. Further, India’s first indigenous 
Hydrogen Fuel Cell Catamaran Vessel was 
sailed off to Varanasi from CSL, marking a 
major milestone in the country’s journey 
towards sustainable maritime solutions. 
Coming to the ship repair segment, CSL 
successfully handled a total of 187 projects 
across its five ship repair units located along 
the west and east coasts of India. Notably, CSL 
completed the short refit and dry docking of 
INS Vikramaditya, Indian Navy’s aircraft carrier 
and signed the Master Ship Repair Agreement 
(MSRA) with the United States Navy, enabling 
CSL to undertake repairs of US Naval Vessels 
under the Military Sealift Command.  
During the year, CSL organised the Ship 
Design Conclave ‘SANKALP’ under the 
theme ‘Design in India, Design for the 
World’, with the objective of strengthening 
India’s ship design ecosystem and 
promoting indigenous capabilities.
CSL’s Strategic & Advanced 
Solutions Division (C-SAS)
In keeping with industry trends, CSL through 
its Strategic & Advanced Solutions (C-SAS) 
division is trying to tap into emerging 
opportunities. The C-SAS division has made 
good progress during 2024-25. The first 
indigenous Hydrogen Fuel Cell Catamaran 
Vessel has now been deployed at Varanasi 
along with the allied H2 fueling infrastructure. 
After the maiden surface run of the HEAUV 
for DRDO, which met all mission parameters, 
C-SAS is now concentrating on development 
of an autonomous vessel, for which we have 
secured 50% funding under the MoPSW’s 
R&D scheme. By focusing on cutting-edge 
technologies, specialized services, and confidence, Udupi-CSL has built a healthy 
order book of approximately ₹2,200 Crores.
For the year ended March 31, 2025, Udupi-
CSL reported a turnover of ₹26,564 Lakhs, 
compared to ₹17,972 Lakhs in the previous 
year. The Company recorded a profit of ₹263 
Lakhs, against ₹111 Lakhs in the previous year.
Corporate governance 
The Company is committed to comply with 
good corporate governance practices. The 
Company complies with the applicable 
corporate governance regulations of 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015, and also the Guidelines 
on Corporate Governance issued by the 
Department of Public Enterprises except w.r.t 
the appointment of Independent Directors 
and related non-compliances. 
As on March 31, 2025, the Board of CSL did 
not have Independent Directors, including 
a Woman Director, against the statutory 
requirement of six. This situation arose 
following the resignation of Shri Prithiviraj 
Harichandan, Independent Director, with 
effect from May 02, 2024, to contest in the 
Odisha Legislative Assembly elections, and 
the completion of tenure of the remaining 
five Independent Directors on November 
21, 2024. CSL being a CPSE, the power to 
appoint Directors on the Board vests with strategic partnerships, C-SAS is diversifying 
CSL’s portfolio and strengthening our 
competitive edge. 
C-SAS is also spearheading CSL’s ‘USHUS’ 
Maritime Startup Scheme, driving innovation 
by identifying and supporting promising 
startups in the maritime sector. IIM Kozhikode 
LIVE and IIT Madras serve as the Review 
and Recommending Agencies for selection, 
monitoring, and stakeholder coordination. 
To date, ₹5.1 Crores have been committed 
to 11 startups specializing in deep tech, AI, 
renewable energy, and eco-materials.
Subsidiary companies 
Hooghly Cochin Shipyard 
Limited (Hooghly-CSL)
Hooghly-CSL, our wholly owned subsidiary 
at Nazirgunge, West Bengal, continued to 
strengthen its operations during the year. The 
Yard secured an order for two 40T ASD Bollard 
Pull Tugs from Industrial Handling Private 
Limited. This is in addition to the previous 
order for two similar vessels awarded during 
FY 2024. Further, Hooghly-CSL is also building 
six Hybrid Electric Catamaran Passenger 
Vessels for the Inland Waterways Authority of 
India (IWAI) and a 2,200T Multi-Purpose Vessel 
for JAK Maritime & Logistics India Private 
Limited. Alongside these projects, Hooghly-
CSL is serving as consultant to IWAI for setting 
up a new ship repair facility at Pandu, Assam. 
During FY 2024–25, Hooghly-CSL reported a 
turnover of ₹5,775 Lakhs as against ₹2,072 
Lakhs in the previous year. The Company 
recorded a loss of ₹1,738 Lakhs compared to 
a loss of ₹3,006 Lakhs in FY 2023–24. With 
the ongoing execution of these projects, 
the Company remains focused on improving 
operational performance and enhancing 
revenue realisation in the coming years.
Udupi Cochin Shipyard 
Limited (Udupi-CSL)
Udupi-CSL, our wholly owned subsidiary 
based in Udupi, Karnataka, deepened its 
foothold in the small and medium-sized 
vessel segment during FY 2024–25. The 
Yard’s strong execution capabilities led to 
repeat orders from satisfied clients, including 
twelve 70T Bollard Pull Tugs; eleven from 
Ocean Sparkle Limited and one from Polestar 
Maritime Limited and eight 6,300 TDW Dry 
Cargo Vessels from Wilson ASA, Norway. 
With consistent performance and customer I am pleased to share that CSL achieved its
highest-ever turnover, PBT and PAT both in
terms of standalone and consolidated basis in
the financial year 2024–25, marking another
significant milestone in the Company’s growth
journey.Udupi-CSL ’s strong 
execution capabilities 
led to repeat orders 
from satisfied clients, 
including twelve 70T 
Bollard Pull Tugs; 
eleven from Ocean 
Sparkle Limited and one 
from Polestar Maritime

TDW Dry Cargo Vessels 
from Wilson ASA, 
Norway.

applicable regulations.Human resource 
At CSL, we view our people as the 
foundation of our success. As on March 31, 
2025, our total manpower stood at 3,542, 
complemented by 1,083 trainees who are 
undergoing structured on-the-job training 
at the Yard. During the year, 1,310 new 
hires were onboarded across categories 
including trainees, in line with our growing 
operational footprint. To build capabilities 
across all levels, we conducted over 200 
training programmes totaling around 4,650 
mandays, both in house and at premier 
institutions. These programmes focused on 
technical, safety, functional and leadership 
domains benefitting more than 3,350 
participants. It is worthwhile to note that a 
total of 40 employees attended a customized 
training program in Japan, conducted in 
two batches during April 2024 and February 
2025, with 50% women participation in 
the second batch, reflecting our strong 
focus on up-skilling and promoting gender 
diversity in the workforce. Emphasizing the 
need for continuous learning and leadership 
development, CSL introduced its leadership 
talk series, Prajyoti and Prajnan. These 
sessions are designed to inspire and engage 
the workforce through short talks delivered 
by reputed personalities from various fields. 
As part of this initiative, 4 sessions of Prajyoti 
and 3 sessions of Prajnan were conducted 
during the financial year 2024-25. CSL also 
implemented progressive HR reforms this 
year, including provisions for Child Care 
Leave and Critical Illness Leave, reaffirming 
our commitment to building a caring and 
inclusive workplace. CSL also continued its 
employee welfare efforts through schemes 
like Employees Medical Assistance Scheme, 
Employees Pension Scheme, Shipyard Parivar 
Prathibha Puraskar Scheme, Employees 
Educational Assistance Scheme etc.
Industrial relations 
CSL maintained a harmonious industrial 
relations environment during FY 2024–25, 
with no loss of man-hours due to labour 
unrest attributable to the Company. 
Employees across all levels, including 
executives, non-unionised supervisors 
and workmen, continued to demonstrate 
dedication, discipline and alignment with the 
Company’s objectives. Mutually respectful 
relationship between Management, 
Trade Unions, associations and various 
stakeholders, always making sure that CSL 
will be at the core of our thinking, has been a 
hallmark of CSL.
CSL also cares deeply for its retired 
employees, continuing to provide cashless medical benefits to over 2,000 retired 
employees and their eligible dependents and 
additionally providing medicines to about 
850. In addition to the medical scheme, CSL 
also provides financial support to retired 
employees through various schemes. This 
includes support to 33 retired employees 
under the ‘Shipyard Aswasa Kiranam’ and 
‘Shipyard Santhwana Sparsham’ schemes. 
Further, to honour the invaluable services 
of those who retired before 2007, CSL 
introduced the ‘Sayam Prabha’ scheme, 
under which cash gifts are presented to 
retired employees on their 75th birthday and 
every five years thereafter. A total of 307 
employees have been honoured with cash 
gifts under this scheme. 
Through its ongoing engagement and support 
measures, the Company upheld a stable and 
collaborative work environment that enabled 
progress across its operations .
Sustainability 
At CSL, our aim is to embed sustainability 
into every facet of our operations. We 
recognise that the future of shipbuilding 
lies in adopting practices that are both 
environmentally responsible and operationally 
efficient. In addition to building green ships, 
CSL is also working towards switching to 
100% clean energy for its operations soon, 
aiming to become the first Indian shipyard 
run entirely by green power. Our leadership 
in sustainability is further recognized with 
an upgrade to the ‘Gold’ rating in the CII 
GreenCo framework. Beyond green energy, 
CSL’s focus on Environmental, Social, and 
Governance (ESG) principles is integral to our 
future strategy. 
CSL remains fully aligned with the nation’s 
broader sustainability goals and we will 
continue to invest in cleaner technologies, 
renewable energy and eco-efficient 
infrastructure to ensure our operations remain 
future-ready and environmentally responsible.
Safety
Safety remains a core organisational priority 
at CSL, reflected in our structured systems, 
continuous training and commitment to 
international standards. The Company 
maintains an Integrated Management System 
(IMS) in line with ISO 9001:2015 Quality 
Management, ISO 14001:2015 Environmental 
Management and ISO 45001:2018 
Occupational Health & Safety Management, 
ensuring compliance with best-in-class 
HSE practices. In March 2025, CSL further 
strengthened its framework by obtaining 
ISO 27001:2022 certification for establishing and maintaining an Information Security 
Management System (ISMS).
To strengthen safety awareness and capacity-
building, CSL operates a dedicated HSE 
Competency Development Centre that offers 
structured training to our workforce. The 
Company continued to invest in various HSE 
initiatives across all operational areas during 
FY 2024–25. CSL also conducts regular safety 
audits, inspections and risk assessments 
as part of its commitment to proactively 
identifying and mitigating potential hazards at 
all levels. During the year, CSL also organised 
a two-day HSE Conclave ‘SAMSRAYA’ under 
the theme ‘Leading Indian Shipyards to 
Global Best Practices’, inaugurated by Shri T K 
Ramachandran IAS, Secretary, Ministry of 
Ports, Shipping and Waterways. The conclave 
brought together leading shipyards from 
across the country to share best practices 
and strengthen the culture of safety in 
shipbuilding and ship repair.
CSL’s efforts in safety management were 
recognised at multiple forums during the 
year. The Company won the Kerala Industrial 
Safety Award 2024 (Sub Category II) from 
the Department of Factories and Boilers, 
Government of Kerala. CSL was also honoured 
with the ‘Sreshta Suraksha Puraskar’ for 
Outstanding Safety Performance in the Very 
Large Factories – Engineering category by the 
National Safety Council (Kerala Chapter). In 
addition, the Company secured the second 
prize from the National Safety Council (Kerala 
Chapter) for excellence in contractor safety 
management systems.
CSR
CSL remains committed to its role as a 
responsible corporate citizen, aligning 
its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) 
initiatives with national priorities. A structured 
CSR framework is in place, supported by 
a dedicated CSR Cell that ensures proper 
planning, execution, and monitoring of 
projects approved by the Board. Over the 
years, CSL has implemented more than 900 
projects across India, with a cumulative 
CSR spent of over ₹140 Crores, focusing on 
healthcare, education, skilling, environmental 
sustainability, and community development. 
During the financial year, the Company 
spent ₹17.90 Crores against the mandated 
budget of ₹13.88 Crores, implementing 108 
CSR projects with Health & Nutrition and 
PM Internship Scheme as the central theme. 
In line with DPE directives, Wayanad, an 
aspirational district with a significant tribal 
population, was a key focus area. CSR projects 
were undertaken not only in Kerala but also 
in other parts of the country, including the north-eastern states. I am happy to report 
that CSL was honoured with two awards for 
its CSR performance—one by the National 
Institute of Personnel Management (NIPM), 
Kochi Chapter, and another by the Federation 
of Indian Chambers of Commerce and 
Industry (FICCI) in recognition of its impactful 
CSR initiatives. 
Looking ahead 
As we look ahead, CSL enters the new 
financial year with a strong order book 
of around ₹21,000 Crores, providing 
visibility and stability across defence, 
commercial, and green vessel segments in 
both domestic and international markets. 
Across the CSL group, we have a total of 75 
vessels on order, with 50 currently under 
construction which includes 28 at CSL, 
and 11 each at Hooghly–CSL and Udupi–
CSL respectively.
Our enhanced infrastructure, including 
the new Dry Dock and International Ship 
Repair Facility, has strengthened our ability 
to execute large and complex projects, 
positioning CSL as a reliable partner of 
choice for global clients.
To effectively implement the Government’s 
maritime vision under Maritime India 
Vision (MIV) 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal 
Vision (MAKV) 2047, the Ministry of Ports, 
Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW) has 
established over 20 ViBhaS and NAVIC Cells. 
CSL, plays an active role, with its officers 
involved in 21 such cells—contributing 
strategically to the nation’s maritime 
roadmap. In alignment with national 
initiatives such as the MIV 2030, MAKV 
2047, and India’s goal of becoming a 
developed nation by 2047, CSL has drawn 
up a strategic roadmap viz., CRUISE 20302.0 
to reinforce its role in this transformative 
journey. Leveraging our five decades of 
experience in shipbuilding and ship repair, 
together with expanded infrastructure, 
emerging global maritime trends and the 
Government ‘s policy support, CSL is poised 
to deliver sustainable, technologically 
advanced, and globally competitive 
solutions in the maritime sector.
Our strategy CRUISE 20302.0 is built on two 
pillars – revenue generation and operational 
excellence. Key initiatives identified under 
this roadmap include establishing strategic 
partnerships in large vessel construction, 
establishment of ship repair clusters, 
advancing marine electrification technologies, and exploring international 
collaborations in ship design. These 
initiatives, some of which are already at 
advanced stages of discussion, reflect our 
focus on building capabilities that will not 
only strengthen our competitiveness but 
also contribute meaningfully to the growth 
of India’s maritime sector.
Closing remarks 
In closing, I extend my sincere gratitude 
to the entire team of CSL group for their 
dedication, professionalism and ability to 
deliver excellence across all areas of our 
operations. I would also like to thank our 
valued customers, business partners and 
investors for their trust and continued 
association with the Company. 
I sincerely appreciate the cooperation and 
encouragement extended by the Ministry 
of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Ministry 
of Defence, various Government of India 
departments, and the State Governments 
of Kerala, West Bengal, Maharashtra, 
Karnataka, as well as the Andaman and 
Nicobar Administration, who have been 
instrumental in realizing our aspirations.
As we move forward, we remain consistent 
in our mission to strengthen India’s 
maritime capabilities through innovation, 
sustainability and operational excellence. 
Backed by our robust order book, modern 
infrastructure and skilled workforce, CSL is 
confident of navigating the opportunities 
and challenges of the future, delivering 
long-term value to our stakeholders 
and contributing meaningfully to the 
nation’s growth story.
Thank You, Jai Hind.

Operational excellence
Engineering Efficiency 
Below Deck and Beyond
We operate strategically located shipbuilding and repair facilities across 
India, each aligned to meet specific customer and segment requirements. Our 
infrastructure footprint is tailored to handle complex naval platforms, large 
commercial ships and inland/coastal vessels, supported by a strong emphasis 
on productivity, quality and delivery timelines. These facilities continue to 
reinforce our position as a dependable partner for maritime stak eholders.
Kochi, KeralaMumbai, Maharashtra
Our Kochi operations form the core of our shipbuilding and repair 
capabilities. Equipped with state-of-the-art infrastructure, the 
unit has a proven track record, having delivered over 175 vessels 
of different types and executed more than 2,500 ship repair 
projects. The successful construction and delivery of India’s first 
Indigenous Aircraft Carrier ‘INS Vikrant’ stands as a testimony to 
our technical excellence. The recently added New Large Dry Dock 
and the International Ship Repair Facility (ISRF), has significantly 
expanded our capabilities. The New Large Dry Dock equips us to 
handle strategic assets like future aircraft carriers upto 70,000T 
displacement as also large commercial vessels including Capesize & 
Suezmax vessels, Jack-up rigs, LNG vessels etc. The ISRF is expected 
to modernise and expand our existing ship repair capabilities and 
aspires to transform Kochi as a global ship repair hub. We cater 
to a wide range of domestic and global clients across defence, 
commercial and offshore segments.Our operations in Mumbai are anchored by the CSL Mumbai 
Ship Repair Unit (CMSRU), located at Mumbai Port. Since 
commencing operations in January 2019, the facility has 
successfully completed repair works for over 125 vessels. With 
its growing capabilities, CMSRU has strengthened our presence 
along the western coast, reinforcing our reputation for reliable 
and timely ship repair services. CMSRU undertook a total of 22 
ship repair projects and generated a revenue of ₹177 Crores 
during the financial year 2024-25.
CSL Mumbai Ship Repair Unit 
(CMSRU)
Dry Dock: 300 × 30 × 9 Mtr
Berth: 1 KM (for afloat repairs)
Kolkata, West Bengal
The CSL Kolkata Ship Repair Unit (CKSRU) caters to the ship 
repair needs of the eastern coast, serving both commercial 
and defence segments. Strategically located at Syama Prasad 
Mookerjee Port, the facility commenced operations in October 
2019 and has since completed several significant projects. 
CKSRU continues to deliver consistent, high-quality repair 
solutions with a commitment to operational excellence. During 
the financial year 2024-25, CKSRU has handled 6 refit projects 
and earned a revenue of ₹41 Crores. 
CSL Kolkata Ship Repair Unit 
(CKSRU)
Dry Dock: 172 × 23 × 8 Mtr (2 numbers)
Sri Vijaya Puram, Andaman 
and Nicobar Islands
The CSL Andaman & Nicobar Ship Repair Unit (CANSRU), 
located at the Marine Dockyard in Sri Vijaya Puram (formerly, 
Port Blair), began operations in November 2021. The unit has 
been instrumental in building a robust ship repair ecosystem 
for the region, offering modern, efficient services to meet 
local maritime requirements. During the financial year 2024-
25, CANSRU handled around 25 major repair projects along 
with numerous emergency minor repair activities, generating a 
revenue of ₹186 Crores.

Infra Project highlights
Strategic Assets & Engineering 
Marvels on a Sea of Progress
During the year, we added two mega infrastructure facilities that mark a 
transformative step in our capacity expansion journey. Both the New Large 
Dry Dock and the International Ship Repair Facility (ISRF) were inaugurated 
in January 2024 by the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, reinforcing our role in 
advancing India’s maritime capabilities and supporting national self-reliance in 
shipbuilding and ship repair.
New Large Dry Dock
Analogy and tidbits about 
the ProjectLocated within our existing premises, 
this dry dock facility is engineered to 
handle construction and repairs of 
some of the largest vessel classes, 
thereby significantly strengthening our 
infrastructure readiness for handling 
future defence and commercial vessels. 
Constructed at a cost of ₹1,799 Crores,  70,000 MT of steel forms used – 10 
times the quantity of steel used 
in Eiffel Tower.
 7.2 Lakh Tonnes of concrete used – 
1.25 times concrete quantity used in 
Bandra Worli Sea Link.
 Can hold 242 Million litres of water – 
Equivalent to 95 Nos. of Olympic size 
swimming pools.
 Massive Dewatering Pumps which 
 can dewater the dock in 3.5 hrs.
 5,000 Nos. of RCC piles – Almost 26 
times the number of piles installed 
in Burj Khalifa.
 5,50,000 cu.m. of excavated material 
disposed to sea – Equivalent to 
relaying 300 Nos. of football fields.
 Electrical Cables runs almost 80 Kms.
 Service Pipe Lines runs almost 20 Kms.
 Achieved more than 22 million safe 
manhours.International Ship Repair 
Facility (ISRF)
The ISRF, constructed at a cost 
of ₹970 Crores, consists of a ship 
lift & transfer system of 6000 T 
capacity suitable for handling 
vessels of maximum size: 130 Mtr x 
26 Mtr. It has 6 Work stations which 
would facilitate independent and 
simultaneous repair of six vessels, 
thereby enabling the facility to 
handle repairs of around 82 ships 
a year. The ISRF is expected to 
augment our ship repair capacity 
as well as in establishing Kochi as a 
global destination for ship repairs.

Environment
Eco-Stewardship: Our 
Compass to the Future
We are committed to advancing environmental sustainability 
across our operations by adopting cleaner energy alternatives, 
improving efficiency and encouraging eco-conscious behaviour 
within our workforce. Our focus remains on reducing emissions, 
optimising resource consumption and investing in technologies 
that support a greener future.
Energy conservation 
initiatives
Renewable energy usageTo drive meaningful improvements in 
energy efficiency, we implemented a 
range of targeted interventions across 
our facilities. These included the in-
house conversion of a diesel-powered 
platform truck into an electric variant, 
alongside the procurement of electric 
forklifts to replace older conventional 
models. Our operations also benefited 
from the installation of IoT-based remote 
energy monitoring systems, enabling 
real-time optimisation and minimisation 
of energy waste.
We installed sensor-based lighting in our 
Ship Repair Service Tunnel, electrified 
new buildings with high-efficiency LED 
lighting, and replaced conventional air 
conditioning units with inverter-based 
systems. Additional initiatives included 
installing BLDC motor-based fans and 
man coolers, fixing compressed air and 
gas leaks, maintaining near-unity power 
factor and switching off air compressors 
during idle periods.
We also promoted energy awareness 
across the organisation through 
posters, seminars, and competitions, 
fostering a culture of responsibility and 
sustainability.We continued to reduce our dependency 
on conventional energy sources by 
expanding the use of solar power. Our 
existing rooftop solar plants generated 
clean energy during the year, and we 
additionally procured green power 
through Open Access mechanisms. As 
part of our long-term sustainability 
vision, we are actively working towards 
transitioning to 100% green energy, with 
the goal of becoming the first Indian 
shipyard powered entirely by green 
energy. To achieve this, we are planning 
a hybrid renewable energy project—
combining wind and solar along with 
expanding our rooftop solar capacity, 
enabling us to generate sufficient green 
energy to suffice our consumption. Estimated energy savings from 
conservation measures2.60 Lakh units
Energy generated from installed 
solar capacity of 1672 kWp 
(installed capacity as on  
March 2025)16.83 Lakh units

via Open Access (Green Day

Dividend
4. As per Office Memorandum F.No.5/2/2016-Policy 
dated November 18, 2024 issued by the Department 
of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM), 
every CPSE have to pay a minimum annual dividend of 
30% of PAT or 4% of the networth, whichever is higher. 
Accordingly, your Directors are pleased to recommend a 
final dividend of H2.25 per share on the 26,30,80,780 fully 
paid equity shares of H5 each. Earlier, interim dividends of 
H4 and H3.50, aggregating to H7.50 per equity share had 
been paid to the shareholders during 2024-25. Thus, the total dividend for the year 2024-25 is H9.75 per equity 
share (195%), amounting to H256.50 Crores. No unclaimed 
dividends (previous years’) were due to be transferred to 
the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) during 
the reporting period. 
Offer for Sale (OFS)
5. During October 2024, the Government of India had carried 
out Offer for Sale (OFS) of equity shares of the Company, 
divesting 4.95% of its stake, equivalent to 1,30,15,689 
equity shares, through the stock exchange mechanism, 
in accordance with the applicable SEBI Regulations. 
Consequently, the shareholding of the Government of 
India in CSL came down to 67.91%.
Dividend Distribution Policy
6. As per Regulation 43A of the Securities and Exchange Board 
of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 the top 1000 listed entities shall 
formulate a dividend distribution policy. Accordingly, 
dividend distribution policy has been adopted to set out 
the parameters and circumstances that will be taken into 
account by the Board in determining the distribution of 
dividend to its shareholders and/ or retaining the profit 
into the business. The policy is available on the website 
of the Company at the link https://cochinshipyard.in/
investor/investor_titles/68. 
Raising funds through Blue Bonds
7. To support the Company’s commitment to a 100% green 
transition, CSL plans to raise funds through the issuance of 
blue bonds – a first-of-its-kind initiative by an Indian Public 
Sector Undertaking (PSU). The Board at its meeting held on 
November 07, 2024 approved the proposal for raising funds 
by way of issuance of US$ denominated non-convertible 
senior unsecured fixed rate notes (“Notes”) for an aggregate 
amount up to US$ 50 million, primarily to finance Company’s 
eligible sustainable projects or other permissible end uses 
in accordance with applicable law. CSL plans to list the 
same in any one or more exchanges overseas or in Gujarat 
International Finance Tec-City. The proposal is currently 
pending with the Administrative Ministry for approval.

undertaken repairs of around 126 vessels since

government agencies and Indian Coast Guard, as well as minor/ major repairs for various commercial clients 
totaling a revenue of H177.04 Crores.

25 include the dry dock repair of DSS Vessel ‘MV Swaraj 
Dweep’ and the short refit of the first Coast Guard vessel 
at CKSRU, ‘ICGS Samudra Paheredar’. CKSRU earned a total 
revenue of H41.11 Crores for FY25. A comprehensive H50 
Crores upgrade plan for the repair facility at NSD has been 
developed and implemented over a five-year duration since 
its commencement. Key infrastructure enhancements, 
including the installation of an intermediate dock gate, a 
tower crane and a ring main fire system, have already been 
completed during the financial year 2024-25. 
14. During the financial year 2024-25, CANSRU completed 
dry dock repairs for 14 vessels and undertook 11 afloat 
repairs, in addition to numerous emergency minor repair 
activities. These efforts resulted in a remarkable turnover 
of H185.58 Crores.

CSL Strategic & Advanced Solutions (C-SAS)
17. In order to tap new revenue generation streams beyond 
the current Shipbuilding & Ship Repair portfolios, a

Solutions (C-SAS) was formed to enable the Company

‘SANKALP’ – Design Conclave
18. CSL organised a one-day Design Conclave ‘SANKALP’ in 
October 2024 under the theme ‘Design in India, Design 
for the World’, aimed at fostering a robust ship design 
ecosystem in India. Shri T K Ramachandran IAS, Secretary, 
Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW), 
Government of India, virtually inaugurated the event. 
19. The Conclave served as a vital platform for bringing together 
key stakeholders from across the ship design ecosystem, 
including major shipyards, ship design houses, classification 
societies, the Indian Navy, statutory authorities, and 
esteemed academic and research institutions such as CEMS, 
IITs, and IMU. Through focused sessions and collaborative 
discussions, the Conclave explored various key initiatives 
to drive innovation, strengthen indigenous capabilities, 
and shape the future of ship design in India. The valuable 
insights and actionable recommendations that emerged 
from the Conclave have been compiled and submitted to 
the Ministry for further consideration and action.Expansion Projects
20. The status of major projects and initiatives are as follows:
 (i) International Ship Repair Facility (ISRF) at Cochin 
Port Premises
  Hon’ble Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi 
inaugurated the ISRF project on January 17, 2024. 
6000 T lifting capacity shiplifit system supplied by 
Syncrolift AS, Norway was commissioned and the 
first vessel docking on the shiplift platform was 
carried out. The ISRF is equipped with 6000 T shiplift, 
six workstations and approximately 1400 metre of 
berths; suitable for handling vessels of maximum 130 
metre length. The Facility can repair six such vessel at 
the dry-workstations simultaneously. As on March 31, 
2025, 10 ships were taken at ISRF for repair works.
  Further, ten globally renowned firms in the maritime 
industry have already partnered with CSL for setting 
up their units in the Maritime Park in first phase, and 
five firms started their operations. CSL expects to 
position Kochi as a major ship repair hub with the 
commissioning of the ISRF.
 (ii) New Dry Dock
  Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi 
inaugurated the New Dry Dock on January 17, 2024. 
This state-of-the-art facility, measuring 310 x 75/60 
x 13 meters and equipped with a 600-Ton gantry 
crane, is situated at the northern end of the existing 
premises of the Company at Kochi. The New Dry Dock 
will augment the Company’s shipbuilding and ship 
repair capacity essentially required to tap the market 
potential of building specialized and technologically 
advanced vessels such as LNG carriers, aircraft carriers 
of higher capacity, jack up rigs, drill ships, large 
dredgers and repairing of offshore platforms and 
larger vessels. The testing and commissioning of the 
600-Ton gantry crane were successfully completed 
on February 11, 2025. The Company carries out 
the shipbuilding activities simultaneously in grand 
assembly area and dock floor of the New Dry Dock.

Employee Welfare Measures
51. Child Care Leave – From the calendar year 2025, those 
employees (Executives, Supervisors or Workmen) with 
two (2) years of regular service in CSL shall be eligible for 
Child Care Leave (CCL) up to two (2) years (i.e. 730 days). 
All women employees with dependent disabled children 
(40% or more disability) are eligible for CCL without age 
restrictions. All single parents (male or female) with minor 
dependent children (up to 18 years old) are also eligible 
for CCL for purposes such as exams or sickness during the 
entire service.
52. Employee Welfare Crowd Funding Scheme – CSL has 
launched an Employee Welfare Crowd Funding Scheme 
“Cochin Shipyard Employees Parivar Parirakshan Yojana 
(SEPPY)” in order to support the bereaved family of an 
employee at the event of death of an employee. The 
scheme operates in such a way that an amount of H 600 
will be collected from each employee on the rolls of the 
Company in the event of death of a regular employee. As 
per the scheme, the Company will provide financial support 
at the rate of 1.5 times of fund collected through employee 
crowd funding, subject to a limit of H15,00,000 in the event 
of each natural death case. The maximum benefit provided 
to the dependents through the scheme shall be H25,00,000. 
53. Enhancement of relief under Cochin Shipyard Employees 
Mutual and Public Welfare Trust (CSEMPWT) – CSL 
enhanced the financial death relief to H8,00,000 and funeral 
expenses to H25,000 to the dependents of the members of 
the trust at the event of death of an employee. 
54. Welfare assistance & special casual leave for the care of 
differently abled children – CSL is granting monthly welfare 
assistance of H 4,500 to all permanent employees who are 
having differently abled wards. They are also given time off 
for taking care of the ward in emergency situations limited 
to a maximum of 5 special casual leaves in a calendar year.
55. Modified CSL Medical Assistance Scheme – CSL has modified 
the medical assistance scheme for employees by empanelling 
34 hospitals (Super-specialty/ multi-specialty/ specialty

57. Infertility treatment scheme was launched in the year 
2020 for providing reimbursement of medical expenses 
incurred for infertility treatment for all permanent 
employees. An amount not exceeding H1,00,000 per 
cycle or the actual cost whichever is lower is permitted 
for reimbursement and the same will be allowed up to 
maximum of three fresh cycles with prior approval. Special 
Leave for maximum 10 days in a year and maximum of 20 
days are being granted during the service of an employee 
who undergo procedures as part of infertility treatment. 
A total of 27 employees were granted permission to avail 
the benefits under this scheme as on March 2025.
58. National Pension System (NPS) was introduced in CSL 
in order to facilitate contributory pension scheme for 
all permanent employees. CSL is contributing 10% of 
the wages (Basic + DA) to the individual account of the 
employees, as employer contribution from April 2021 
onwards. The scheme provides attractive income tax 
benefits to the employees and also ensures a hassle-free 
life post retirement.
59. CSL introduced paternity leave in the year 2019 to male 
employees of the Company including for valid adoption of 
a child below the age of one year.
60. CSL as a ‘people first and people caring organisation’ felt the 
necessity to support the employees availing leaves owing to 
rare and extra ordinary circumstances such as treatment 
for cancer, organ failure and organ transplantation. From 
the calendar year 2023, 180 days of Special Leave during 
the service period has been sanctioned to all regular 
employees for undergoing treatment of cancer like surgery, 
chemotherapy or organ failure or donation of organ. There are also cases reported where the dependents of employees 
are in the similar situation and the employees have to avail 
leave to take care of them. As a support for the ailing family 
members, special leave can also be availed by employees for 
the days required for chemotherapy, organ transplantation 
of their dependents.
61. It has also been noted that a number of CSL employees 
are donating blood to the needy as a noble act and a life-
saving gesture. All regular employees are also allowed to 
avail Special Leave for one day for donating blood, subject 
to a maximum of three occasions in a year.

Risk Management
85. CSL has put in place a comprehensive Risk Management 
Policy, approved by the Board of Directors at their 214th 
meeting held on September 16, 2014 and later amended 
at the 259th Board Meeting held on February 12, 2021. 
The Company's risk management policy aims to establish 
a structured and defined process for the identification, 
assessment, response, monitoring and reporting of risks.
48
COCHIN SHIPYARD LIMITED
=== page 33 ===
86. As per the Policy, the CSL Board undertakes overall 
oversight of the risk management system. The Board 
periodically reviews the risk management process to 
ensure that key risks are being properly identified and 
effectively managed. The CSL management, comprising 
both Board-level and below-Board-level executives, 
has been entrusted with the implementation of the 
risk management process. To this end, CSL has set up 
functional Risk Management Committees and a Board-
level Risk Management Committee to implement the 
Risk Management Policy across the organization. These 
committees regularly review the risk management process 
and the Policy to ensure their continued effectiveness. 
In line with the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015, CSL had a Board-
level Risk Management Committee (RMC) to oversee 
the Company's overall corporate risk management till 
November 21, 2024. However, the Committee could 
not be reconstituted thereafter due to the absence of 
Independent Directors on the Board. The Committee will 
be reconstituted once sufficient number of Independent 
Directors are appointed by the Government of India.
87. The diversified product mix of CSL, which includes both 
defense and commercial shipbuilding, as well as ship repair, 
provides the Company with a natural hedge against market 
risks. This diversification helps to mitigate the Company's 
exposure to fluctuations in any particular market segment, 
thereby enhancing the overall resilience of the business.
Health, Safety & Environment (HSE)
88. At CSL, our dedication to exemplary Health, Safety and 
Environment (HSE) standards remains paramount, ensuring 
the safety and well-being of our employees, customers 
and stakeholders. We cultivate a proactive HSE culture, 
underpinned by a meticulously designed management 
system focused on identifying and mitigating potential 
hazards. We recognize that a secure and healthy work 
environment is integral to the overall welfare and success 
of all our stakeholders.
89. We are delighted to announce a significant increase of 8.9% 
in our Organizational HSE Index percentage compared to 
the preceding year of 2023. Efforts towards Health, Safety 
and Environment (HSE) continued to yield significant 
positive outcomes, demonstrating the effectiveness of our 
robust HSE governance system in proactively mitigating 
incidents and accidents. This dedication to proactive 
measures, rather than reactive responses, is clearly 
reflected in our overall and departmental level HSE Index, 
which serves as a key benchmark for our HSE performance 
and reinforces our commitment to safety at all functional 
levels within the organization.90. In May 2024, CSL organized ‘SAMSRAYA’, a significant two-
day Safety Conclave focused on fortifying safety standards 
within India's shipbuilding and ship repair sector. Inaugurated 
by Shri T K Ramachandran IAS, Secretary, Ministry of Ports, 
Shipping and Waterways, Government of India, the event 
aimed to advance HSE practices in the maritime domain 
and explore frameworks for Indian shipyards. Featuring 
dignitaries and experts from India and abroad, including 
representatives from DGFASLI, F&B (Government of Kerala), 
PESO, BIS, Indian Navy, classification societies and leading 
shipyards, the conclave facilitated knowledge exchange and 
collaboration, aligning with the Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 
2047. The successful event underscored CSL's commitment 
to championing safety excellence and driving positive 
change in the industry.
91. The frequency rate of CSL for the year 2024 stands at 
0.13. This metric is closely monitored as a pivotal indicator 
of the Company’s HSE performance. CSL attributes this 
achievement to the Company’s proactive approach and 
the enhancements in overall reporting culture.
92. CSL’s collaborative approach involves ensuring 
subcontractors are well-resourced and trained for 
safe task execution. Continuous HSE performance 
monitoring and constructive feedback remain integral to 
fostering improvement. Recognizing the critical role of 
subcontractors in maintaining high safety standards, CSL’s 
robust evaluation process ensures ongoing alignment with 
CSL's HSE benchmarks and regulator y requirements.
93. The HSE Star rating system, which evaluates the annual 
HSE performance of subcontractors employing 20 or 
more personnel within the Yard on a calendar year basis, 
remained a key mechanism in this endeavor. This rating 
system allows CSL to monitor and encourage continuous 
improvement in HSE standards across stakeholders. These 
ratings, ranging from three star to five star, are a testament 
to the rigorous standards upheld by CSL’s subcontractors. 
23 subcontractors were awarded with CSL HSE Ratings. 
CSL has a dedicated Competency Development Centre 
(CDC) for HSE to achieve HSE learning objectives via 
streamlined training delivery.

(CVC) guidelines are discussed with the heads of

vigilance, emphasis is given to vigilance sensitization 
among the officers and supervisors.

the Vigilance Department. The department also includes 
a Vigilance Officer (DySP rank police officer from Kerala 
Police) on deputation to CSL, two CSL officers, and three 
supporting staff. The Chief Vigilance Officer also oversees 
the vigilance functions of CSL’s wholly owned subsidiaries, 
Hooghly Cochin Shipyard Limited (Hooghly-CSL) and Udupi 
Cochin Shipyard Limited (Udupi-CSL).

Department conducted intensive type examinations and 
recommended various systemic improvements based 
on the findings. CTE-type inspections were carried out 
on select major works and procurements in the Civil 
Department, Ship Building, and Ship Repair divisions. 
During the financial year, the department monitored 
various contracts and audit reports and conducted 
surprise/ periodic inspections in different operational 
areas, suggesting corrective actions wherever necessary.

Annexure I
A. Conservation of Energy 
a. Steps taken or impact on 
conservation of energy 
during the year 2024-25:Steps Taken
	 In-house conversion of a diesel-powered Platform Truck (Jumbo) into an electric powered 
one to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, lower operating costs and minimizes noise 
pollution while improving overall performance and reliability. Materials and components 
available in the Yard were used for the same.
	 Procured two electric forklifts to replace conventional diesel models, offering significant 
advantages such as reduced greenhouse gas emissions, lower maintenance costs, quieter 
operation and enhanced energy efficiency.
	 Implemented an IoT-based remote energy monitoring system to optimize energy utilization, 
enabling real-time tracking that helps minimiz e energy waste.
	 Installed sensor-based lighting controls in the Ship Repair Service Tunnel to improve 
energy efficiency by automatically adjusting lighting based on occupancy, reducing energy 
consumption while enhancing safety and convenience.
	 Completed the electrification of new buildings with the installation of high-efficiency LED 
lighting, significantly reducing energy consumption, lowering maintenance costs.
	 Replaced old air conditioning units with inverter-based AC systems which ensure more 
efficient utilisation of compressors, thus offering more efficient cooling.
	  Installed BLDC motor-based and 5-star rated ceiling fans and man coolers, leveraging the 
efficiency of BLDC technology over traditional induction motors, which reduces energy 
consumption by eliminating mechanical brushes, minimizing heat generation and ensuring 
smoother, more reliable performance.
	 Regularly monitored and repaired leakages in compressed air distribution and industrial gas 
lines to ensure system efficiency, reduce energy loss, and maintain operational reliability.
	 Monitored and maintained the power factor close to unity, ensuring optimal energy 
performance and efficiency by minimizing losses and improving overall system stability.
	 Implemented energy conservation by switching off the main air compressor during 
lunch breaks, maintaining pressure in the receiver tank to prevent unnecessary energy 
consumption during re-pressurization when the compressor is restarted.
	  Promoted energy awareness through various initiatives including posters, stickers, seminars 
and quiz competitions, to encourage responsible electricity usage and foster a culture of 
sustainability across the Yard.
Impact
Energy saving is approx. 2.60 Lakhs units per annum with the implementation of measures 
specified above.
b. Steps taken for utilizing 
alternate sources of 
energy:	 16.83 Lakhs units of energy were generated from existing solar power plants of capacity 
1672 kWp during the year 2024-25.
	 Purchased 49.34 Lakhs units of renewable energy through Open Access (Green Day 
Ahead Market). 
c. Capital investment on 
energy conservation 
equipments:	 An amount of approximately H82 Lakhs have been invested for implementation of energy 
conservation measures specified above.

Annexure II
Report On Corporate Social Responsibility
1. Brief outline on CSR Policy of the Company
 The CSR activities in the Company for the year 2024-25 
were undertaken in line with the statutory provisions under 
the CSR Rules, the guidelines issued by the Department 
of Public Enterprises for Central PSUs and the CSR Policy 
of the Company. 
 As per the CSR Policy of the Company, for administrative 
convenience, the Company operates the projects under 
the categories of Minor projects, which are urgent in 
nature having value of H10 Lakhs or less with the approval 
of Chairman & Managing Director, limited to 10% of total 
spent. All other projects are categorised as Major projects. 
5% of the total spent is earmarked towards administrative 
overheads, which includes salary, expenditure on training 
and travel by CSR staff working in the Department.   Theme for the year: Health & Nutrition and PM 
Internship Scheme
2. Composition of CSR Committee
 The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainable 
Development (CSR & SD) Committee of the Board 
recommends the CSR projects from time to time for the 
approval of the Board. However, effective November 22, 
2024, the CSR & SD Committee ceased to exist due to the 
completion of tenure of the Independent Directors and 
the subsequent non-appointment of new incumbents by 
the Government of India. Accordingly, from November 22, 
2024 onwards, the CSR proposals were considered directly 
by the Board of Directors of the Company based on the 
recommendations of the below Board level CSR Executive 
Committee. The Composition of the CSR & SD Committee 
as on November 21, 2024 is given below:

Report on Corporate Governance
Company’s Philosophy on Corporate Governance
1. Cochin Shipyard recognizes the importance of Corporate Governance to emerge as a model corporate. The Company has 
adopted policies and procedures which are aimed at effectively discharging its responsibilities to various stakeholders, viz., 
shareholders, creditors, customers, employees and society at large. CSL strongly believes that the Company can emerge as a 
strong global leader only by following good & sound Corporate Governance principles. The Company has been rated ‘Excellent’ 
in Corporate Governance practices as per the evaluation criteria prescribed by the Department of Public Enterprises consistently 
for the last several years.
Board of Directors

Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (SEBI Listing Regulations) and the 
Guidelines on Corporate Governance for Central Public Sector Enterprises issued by the Department of Public Enterprises. The

in advance except when it is convened as emergency 
meeting. The agenda notes for each Board/ Committee 
meeting is drafted in consultation with the Chairman and 
are circulated to the Directors not less than seven days in 
advance except when it is convened as emergency meeting 
with the concurrence of all Board/ Committee members. 
All material information is incorporated in the agenda 
papers for facilitating meaningful and focused discussions 
at the meeting. Where it is not practicable to attach any 
document to the agenda, the same is tabled at the meeting 
with specific reference to the subject in the agenda. 
In special and exceptional circumstances, additional or 
supplementary item(s) on the agenda are permitted with 
the consent of all Directors present at the meeting.
20. CSL digitalised its meetings by introduction of a Board 
Management software viz., Dess Digital Meetings, which 
enables to securely create, distribute and manage meeting 
documents in digital format. It ensures that the Board 
and the Committee members get the communication 
at the right time and securely. This Board management 
software will streamline the entire meeting process right 
from the preparation of agenda papers till the finalisation 
of minutes of the meetings, which will in turn save time, 
effort & cost and improve governance.
Recording Minutes of proceedings at Board and 
Committee meeting
21. The Company Secretary records the minutes of the 
proceedings of each Board and Committee meetings. 
Draft minutes are circulated to all the members of the 
Board/ Committee for their comments within fifteen days 
from the conclusion of the meeting. The final minutes 
are entered in the minutes book within 30 days from the 
conclusion of the meeting.
Post Meeting Follow up Mechanism
22. The important decisions taken at the Board/ Committee 
meetings are promptly communicated to the departments/ divisions concerned. The status of implementation of 
major decisions are apprised to the Board/ Committee in 
the ensuing meetings, wherever required.
Compliance
23. The Company Secretary while preparing the agenda notes, 
minutes etc. of the meeting(s) is responsible for and is 
required to ensure adherence to all the applicable laws 
and regulations including the Companies Act, 2013 read 
with the Rules issued thereunder and also the Secretarial 
Standards issued by the Institute of Company Secretaries 
of India and notified by the Government of India.

70. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 124 of the Companies 
Act, 2013 read with the Investor Education and Protection 
Fund Authority (Accounting, Audit, Transfer and Refund) 
Rules, 2016, dividend which remains unpaid/ unclaimed 
for a period of seven years from the date of transfer 
to unpaid dividend account shall be transferred to the 
Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF), a Fund 
constituted by the Central Government under Section 
125 of the Companies Act, 2013. Further, all the shares in 
respect of which dividend has not been paid or claimed for 
seven consecutive years or more shall also be transferred 
in the name of IEPF.

Company at https://cochinshipyard.in/investor/investor_

or unethical practices. Directors/ employees/ stakeholders/

rules, regulations and unethical conduct. The Directors and 
Senior Management are bound to maintain confidentiality

Subsidiary Company
88. Regulation 16 of the SEBI Listing Regulations defines a 
‘material subsidiary’ as subsidiary, whose income or net 
worth exceeds 10% of the consolidated income or net 
worth respectively, of the listed entity and its subsidiaries 
in the immediately preceding accounting year. Under 
this definition, the Company does not have any unlisted 
material subsidiary incorporated in India.
89. Hooghly Cochin Shipyard Limited (Hooghly-CSL) is a wholly 
owned subsidiary company of Cochin Shipyard Limited 
(CSL) which was incorporated as a Joint Venture Company 
on October 23, 2017, venturing with Hooghly Dock & Port 
Engineers Limited. However, since November 01, 2019, 
Hooghly-CSL is a wholly owned subsidiary of CSL. Further, 
CSL acquired Tebma Shipyards Limited through the 
statutory insolvency resolution process on September 15, 
2020, thereby making it a wholly owned subsidiary of CSL. 
Subsequently, on April 22, 2022, Tebma Shipyards Limited 
was renamed as Udupi Cochin Shipyard Limited.

Risk Management Process
101. CSL has put in place a comprehensive Risk Management 
Policy, approved by the Board of Directors at their 214th 
meeting held on September 16, 2014 and later amended 
at the 259th Board Meeting held on February 12, 2021. 
The salient features of the said policy are as follows:
 (i) Risk Management Vision Statement: Minimize the 
organizational risks to an acceptable level and adopt 
risk management practices which would help the 
Company to attain its goals and objectives while at 
the same time ensuring minimization of risks.
 (ii) Risk Management Policy: 
  (a) The risk management process is implemented 
to improve the Company’s ability to prevent 
risks and ensure timely detection of risk.
  (b) To identify risks and its mitigation.
  (c) Risk management process to be standardized.
  (d) Facilitate sharing of risk information.
102. The risk management policy intends to put in place an 
effective risk management framework and an appropriate 
reporting mechanism. The management of Cochin 
Shipyard would periodically identify the various risks 
and assess/ analyze their impact on the Company. Risk 
mitigation and management measures would be put in 
place to effectively manage these risks. The Board may 
approve changes to the policy from time to time in order 
to align it with the changes in business environment.

Risk Management System and Structure
103. The Board has constituted a Risk Management Committee to review the risk management system within CSL. The Board also 
discharge its responsibility of risk oversight by ensuring the review at periodical intervals. The CSL management comprising of 
CSL Board level and below Board level executives are entrusted with the implementation of the risk management process. In 
this respect, Risk Management Steering Committee and Functional Risk Management Committees have been constituted to 
implement the policy in CSL.
104. Due to the peculiar nature of business carried on by CSL, it avoids the risk relating to its commodities.

4. Regarding cargo volumes, last year brought varied performances across different segments. Dry bulk and oil & gas trades 
both decelerated as their growth declined from 3.4% to 1.7% and from 3% to 2.6%, respectively. However, the container liner 
segment saw a significant rebound of 3.8%, approaching levels not seen since 2021 when the world was exiting COVID. The 
global landscape remained unpredictable in 2024 as the Ukrainian war persisted and conflicts in the Middle East continued 
unabated. Houthi attacks in the Red Sea have essentially cut off one of the world’s most crucial and busy waterways between 
East and West. Meanwhile, the US presidential election and declarations of increased tariffs that could lead to economic 
warfare sparked interrogations, although the full impact on shipping markets remains hard to predict and brings uncertainty to 
the future market.
 Source: BRS Annual Review 2025
5. Last year, the shipbuilding market continued to flourish despite increasing delivery times and higher prices that showed no 
signs of weakening. New orders surged by more than 50% (DWT basis) compared with 2023, which had already seen a 37% 
increase on 2022. One striking feature of 2024 was that China significantly grew its order book, boosting its share of the global 
shipbuilding market by 9.7%, further solidifying its dominant position at the expense of Japan (-4.3%) and South Korea (-5.1%). 
Meanwhile, robust market conditions discouraged owners from recycling their older tonnage.
 Source: BRS Annual Review 2025

8. Currently, there are about 348 operational shipyards 
worldwide, having either secured new contracts or 
completed deliveries in the past year. This is roughly 50% 
of 2007’s peak of around 700 active yards. It is noteworthy 
that recent years have seen significant consolidation 
among shipyards. This has reduced the total number of 
active yards but increased overall production capacity, 
while dormant yards are being revitalised and brought 
back into operation.
9. Regarding order book position, China continues to dominate 
the shipbuilding industry, accounting for nearly three-
quarters of global shipbuilding orders. This dominance has 
raised concerns in other nations, prompting discussions 
on revitalizing domestic shipbuilding capabilities. India has 
reaffirmed its presence in the international shipbuilding 
market, climbing in the group of countries other than 
big three (China, Korea, Japan) and Europe from sixth to 
fourth place with 68 ships on order, up from 48 in 2023 and 
30 in 2022. Main contributions being Chowgule Shipyard 
secured six contracts for 10,740 DWT general cargo ships 
for Dutch company Vertom at its new Mangalore facility. 
State-owned Cochin Shipyard won orders for eight 6,375 
DWT general cargo ships for Norway’s Wilson. Mazagon 
Shipyard is building six 7,500 DWT general cargo ships for 
Denmark’s Navi Merchants, while Garden Reach Shipyard 
(GRSE) has four 7,800 DWT dry cargo ships.
10. New building prices for bulkers, tankers and container 
carriers saw only modest increases in 2024. The Chinese 
New building Price Index (CNPI), produced by a panel of shipbuilders and shipbrokers, strengthened by 6% in 2024. 
Individual indices related to bulkers, tankers and container 
carriers, meanwhile, rose by 7%, 7% and 3%, respectively. 
After a slight uptick in the first and second quarters, prices 
stabilised. The booming container market played a key role 
in driving prices up, with second-hand vessel values also 
rising considerably. Meanwhile, shipyard costs have been 
steadily rising. Salaries are up, but the more significant 
factor has been price hikes from suppliers, driven by 
inflation and higher demand. Despite the apparent 
"boom in the market, shipyards are still facing difficulties. 
Growing construction costs seem to be outpacing the rise 
in new building prices, leaving shipyards less satisfied than 
one might expect.
11. Similar to 2024, which was a strong year for ordering 
(second only to 2007), with order books for some segments 
already stretching to 2028 and beyond, 2025 may not be as 
buoyant but there are several factors such as the need to 
meet new environmental rules and regulations, the need 
to replace an ageing fleet and the need to reduce speed 
to comply with intermediate requirements like the CII can 
keep the order book build up to continue. However, there 
remains potential for a new super-cycle in the shipbuilding 
industry to replace the large number of vessels that were 
delivered between 2005 and 2010. 
Indian Shipbuilding Industry and Government 
Initiatives
12. India’s shipbuilding and shipping sectors are undergoing 
strategic transformation under the Government of India’s 
long-term maritime vision. Through the Maritime India 
Vision 2030 (MIV 2030) and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 
2047 (MAKV 2047), the Government has set ambitious targets to elevate India’s position to the 10th largest 
globally in ship owning and shipbuilding by 2030, and 5th 
by 2047. These targets are supported by targeted policy 
interventions and infrastructure development programs. 
13. The Government estimates that an addition of 4–5 million 
gross tonnes (GT) of annual shipbuilding capacity over 
the next 23 years. The cumulative shipbuilding output is 
projected to be valued at USD 237 billion to carry Indian 
cargo, with an additional USD 142 billion in potential 
value addition from ancillary suppliers. Realizing this scale 
will require an estimated investment of approximately 
USD 18 billion across shipbuilding, repair, and ancillary 
sectors. Key policy measures include the Shipbuilding 
Financial Assistance Policy (SBFAP) 2.0, which provides 
financial support to promote domestic ship construction, 
with enhanced incentives for larger, technologically 
advanced, and green vessels operating on alternative 
fuels like ammonia, methanol, hydrogen, and hybrid 
propulsion systems.Newbuilding Price IndexMar-15110120130140150160170180190200Index, Jan’88 = 100
